newsitem.title: ITALY: Mob rakes in money from Albanian exodus to Italy.
newsitem.headline: Mob rakes in money from Albanian exodus to Italy.

text.p: Albanians fleeing their chaotic country in a flotilla of decrepit boats said on Tuesday they had paid racketeers hundreds of dollars to cross the Adriatic to Italy.

As the exodus swelled to 8,000 people in five days, exhausted passengers reaching southeast Italy said they paid the equivalent of $600 each in the port of Durres for places on jam-packed vessels and the chance of a new life abroad.

"I paid and I would pay again if I had to," said Aljosha Sulaj, a 28-year-old businessman who said he had handed over the equivalent of around $3,000 for himself, his wife, his mother-in-law and their young son and baby daughter.
"To get to the port was not easy. At every checkpoint there were people with guns who asked for money and I gave it to them. Then there was no problem getting near the boat," he said.
Concern is growing in Italy that the country could be facing a fresh wave of illegal immigration and crime rather than a genuine refugee crisis.

Sulaj arrived on a rusting cargo boat from Durres that docked in Brindisi with 459 people, some of them reasonably well-dressed. Police said they had found a large hunting knife and a drawerful of bullets in a search of the ship's bridge.
"We sold the car and the house," said Brikena Shpati, 28, who arrived in the port of Otranto with her husband Luan and their two-year-old son on another boat from Durres.
The fee for the trip to Italy is around eight times the average monthly wage in Albania, Europe's poorest country.

Chief anti-Mafia prosecutor Pier Luigi Vigna said he was worried that the influx would import yet more crime, with many of Albania's jails emptied after rioters in the unrest stormed prisons and opened the gates.
"Albania has become the world's first country to have no prisoners," Vigna told Corriere della Sera newspaper.

"The Albanian mafia is running the boats in Durres...Our worry is that, apart from the Albanian mafia, Albanian arms will come in too -- arms that will then become available to the (Italian) mafia," he said.
Italy faced a crisis in 1991 when some 40,000 Albanians commandeered rusting freighters and flooded across the Adriatic after the collapse of 45 years of Stalinist rule.
It has since grappled with continuing problems of illegal Albanian immigration and drugs and arms-smuggling.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government says it will grant temporary sanctuary to genuine refugees from the armed chaos that has swept the country in an eruption of anger over the failure of shady saving schemes.
But with makeshift reception centres in the southeast full to capacity and Albanians being bussed to other regions, the mood in the past two days has turned from sympathy to suspicion.
"This is not a flight of the desperate," La Repubblica newspaper wrote. "This is the emigration of people who hope that they can seize the opportunity to get here and stay."
Milan mayor Marco Formentini of the separatist Northern League party said he would refuse to accommodate any of the Albanians in his city, calling most of them delinquents.
"The state has raised the white flag in the face of an Albanian invasion. Other countries have closed their borders. Italy has opened the sea," he told Corriere della Sera.
